title: Studying Management Is a Real Challenge!

Farhia Jalil 6 min read · Sep 29, 2026 -- 1 Listen Share “Management? It’s just part of business. How hard can it be?” That was exactly what I thought. On the very first day of class, everyone was already talking about our management professor. They said he was incredibly strict. Apparently, he never gave good marks, no matter how hard students tried. But honestly, I never believed that. My perspective was simple: if my answer sheet contains what he’s looking for, why wouldn’t he give me marks? He’s not my enemy — he doesn’t even know me. Surely he’s grading the work, not the person. Little did I know that the real challenge wasn’t the professor. It was management itself. If you’re a management student, you’ve probably heard people say, “Management is easy.” It’s often seen as the degree students choose, to avoid engineering equations, medical textbooks, or endless programming assignments. From the outside, it looks like we’re simply learning how to become future bosses. I used to laugh at those stereotypes too. Then I actually started studying management during this trimester at university. And I realized something surprising. Management isn’t difficult because of complicated formulas or endless memorization. It’s difficult because it requires you to understand one of the most unpredictable systems in existence — people. One statement from my professor completely changed how I looked at education. He said, “I’m not teaching you management. I’m teaching you how to learn… and then relearn.” He explained that what we’re studying today may become outdated in ten or twenty years. The world changes. Businesses change. Technology changes. Human behavior changes. If we want to remain relevant, we have to master the art of relearning. That sentence stayed with me. Back in my A Level Business classes, I thought I already understood management. Looking back now, I realize that what I learned was only a preview. University opened an entirely different world. Then came my first quiz. I did terribly. Honestly, I was disappointed in myself. I kept assuming my IAL Business knowledge was enough instead of trying to relearn management from my professor’s perspective. That assumption cost me. It was a humbling lesson. After the quiz, I went home and started reading the books my professor recommended. I went through his lecture slides again and again. Something unexpected happened. I couldn’t stop studying management. For days, I found myself reaching for my management book instead of my other course books. It almost became addictive. The art of managing people, organizations, and resources fascinated me. I started thinking about companies like Google, Ford Motor Company, Starbucks, and McDonald’s. Without management, none of these organizations would have become what they are today. Technology matters. Capital matters. Innovation matters. But without people who know how to organize those resources, even the greatest ideas would remain just ideas. That’s fascinating. In mathematics, two plus two will always equal four. In chemistry, reactions follow established principles. But in management? The “correct” decision depends on the market, culture, the economy, employees, customer behavior, competitors, timing, ethics, available resources — and sometimes even luck. Twenty students can analyze the same business case and produce twenty completely different solutions. And every one of them could be logically justified. That’s what makes management both fascinating and frustrating. Although, if I’m being honest, the fascination outweighs the frustration. Management isn’t just one subject. It’s an entire ecosystem. One day you’re studying accounting to understand financial health. The next day you’re learning marketing psychology to understand consumers. Then comes economics to predict market behavior. Human resource management teaches motivation. Operations management focuses on efficiency. Business law keeps organizations compliant. Organizational behavior explains why people behave differently inside companies. Strategic management brings everything together. You’re constantly switching perspectives. One day you’re thinking like a financial analyst. The next day you’re thinking like a marketer. Then suddenly you’re solving operational problems while considering legal risks and ethical consequences. Very few disciplines require students to connect so many different fields at the same time. That’s one of the things I enjoy the most. During my IAL Business classes, I was already used to connecting different concepts while analyzing case studies. Management takes that to another level. Now every answer requires you to consider industries, cultures, stakeholders, ethics, psychology, finance, and strategy — all at once. Furthermore, one of the biggest misconceptions about management is that it teaches people how to tell others what to do. Reality couldn’t be more different. Leadership isn’t about authority. It’s about influence. And influence is difficult. How do you motivate employees with completely different personalities? How do you solve conflicts without creating new ones? How do you make unpopular decisions while maintaining trust? How do you balance employee well-being with shareholder expectations? There isn’t a universal formula. Every situation demands judgment.
